chapter_theme: The way of the false guru (அசற்குரு நெறி): the false guru lacks inner feeling and true knowledge, does not see the Veda-Agama path, reviles others, is ruled by lust, and teaches for his food what he has only looked at. Such teaching harms the teacher, the king and the land, and teacher and pupil fall together like the blind leading the blind.
structure_note: Three portraits of the false guru (2044 to 2046), the harm of his teaching to self, king and realm (2047), and the image of the blind (2048).

2044.reading: A fool without inner feeling, who does not ascertain the truth, never sees even a part of the Veda-Agama path, does no service, reviles others and has the nature of a bound soul: he is a false guru.
2044.nuance: பரநிந்தை can be reviling others or reviling the Supreme. அணுவின் குணத்தோன், one with the quality of the anu, is taken as one still in the bound soul's state, who cannot free others. கணுவின்றி is read as 'not even a joint's length'.

2045.reading: Those who have looked over mantra, tantra, great yoga and jnana, bondage and release, yet do not reflect on them or make others clear, and go blind for the sake of food: they are false gurus.
2045.nuance: தரிசித்துப் பார்ப்பவர் suggests acquaintance by sight, without having thought it through (சிந்தனை செய்யா). ஊண்பொருட்டு names the motive: teaching as a living.

2046.reading: He who does not know what is, a fool and a great fool, a wretch not free of lust and the rest, who teaches the unreal to wretches as the way, is without knowledge: he is no master but an unreal teacher.
2046.nuance: அசத்து (the unreal) is a Siddhanta term for what is not abiding; the unreal teacher passes on the unreal. கலதி (wretch, the luckless) is applied to both teacher and pupils.

2047.reading: If one teaches without removing the fancies that pose as learning, one's own state declines and one becomes one's own enemy; it is ruin to the good king and to the land, as Nandi said of old.
2047.nuance: கற்பாய கற்பங்கள் is unclear: கற்பம் may be kalpana (imaginings), ritual prescriptions (kalpa), or a play on கற்பு (learning). தற்பாவம் may be one's own condition or the state of becoming That. The claim that bad teaching ruins king and realm echoes the first tantra's concern with rule.

2048.reading: The blind who go showing the stick to the blind fall, front and back, into the old pit in their way; the blind leader falls, front and back, altogether; the blind fall together with the blind.
2048.nuance: குருடு repeats in every line, so the verse stumbles as its walkers do. The guru who is himself blind is meant, not the pupil alone.

links.note: Both end with blind and blind falling into the pit; 1680 blames the pupils who choose a guru who cannot cure blindness, 2048 the blind guru who shows the stick.

2044 lists the false guru: no inner feeling, not seeing the Veda-Agama path, doing no service, reviling, of the bound soul's nature (அணுவின் குணத்தோன்); 2053 describes the lasting guru (நீடும் குரவன்), stainless, able to give a love free of mala, to those who have grasped the tattvas. Together they set the condition on taking a guru: the bound cannot free, only the mala-free can give.

2045 says false gurus have looked over mantra, tantra, yoga and jnana but do not reflect and do not make others clear (தெளிவியாது), teaching for food; Naladiyar 318 says some fill houses with books without grasping their meaning, and those who understand and make others understand (தேற்றும் புலவர்) are another kind. Both separate possessing the texts from understanding them well enough to make another clear.

2046 calls a false guru one not free of lust and the rest (காமாதி நீங்கா) who teaches the unreal to others; Kural 834 says no fool is greater than one who studies, understands and teaches others (பிறர்க்குரைத்தும்) but does not restrain himself (தானடங்கா). Both condemn the teacher whose own passions are unrestrained; the Tirumanthiram adds that what such a teacher passes on is அசத்து, the unreal.

2047 says teaching without removing the false learning lowers one's own state and brings ruin to the good king and the land (அரசுக்கும் நாட்டுக்கும் கேடு); 241 says if those whose ignorance remains take up tuft and thread, the land withers and the king loses standing. Both tie the fitness of religious teachers to the health of the realm, and 2047 cites Nandi for it.
